solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Marine air private takes on heading to tense favela

indicators.note: a heading sits at the top, so only the opening letter of the next word is wanted

blocks.note: a sea shanty is a sailors' song, a tune of the sea
the opening letter of the word
something private is your own

explanation.surface: A soldier with a sea song on his lips heads into a tense Brazilian slum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like a soldier but is the adjective meaning one's own, which 'takes on' the T. A favela is a Brazilian slum settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: A favela is a Brazilian slum, an informal settlement of makeshift huts, which is exactly what a shantytown is.

clue.text: Sandwiches for people on a bench

blocks.note: first meaning: long submarine-shaped sandwiches
second meaning: substitutes waiting on the sidelines in a team sport

explanation.surface: Packed lunches handed out to people sitting on a bench.
explanation.walkthrough: The bench is a sports bench, where the reserve players sit until called on.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for submarine rolls and for substitutes, the same four-letter word covers both long sandwiches and reserve players.

clue.text: A punter or a pimp?

blocks.note: taken as written
a punter is someone who places bets

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether some shady character is a gambler or a procurer.
explanation.walkthrough: A punter is British slang for a gambler as well as a customer; read A + BETTER, it becomes one who abets.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimp aids and encourages others in wrongdoing, so he is an accomplice who abets crime.

clue.text: How one might describe enemy sapper?

definitions.text: How one might describe enemy sapper?

blocks.clueFragment: How one might describe enemy sapper?
blocks.note: surface reading: a description of a military engineer serving the enemy
setter's reading: time is proverbially the enemy, and something that saps it uses it up

explanation.surface: Someone describing a hostile army engineer who lays mines.
explanation.walkthrough: A sapper is a soldier who digs trenches and mines, but here it just means something that saps; 'the enemy' is the old phrase for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that drains away the hours, wasting a great deal of the clock, is described with this compound adjective.

clue.text: Things many might run in coaches

blocks.note: first meaning: running shoes, in British usage
second meaning: people who coach athletes

explanation.surface: Things many people might dash about in while riding long-distance buses.
explanation.walkthrough: Coaches suggests buses, but it means sports instructors; trainers is the British word for sneakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports shoes worn for jogging, and instructors who prepare athletes, share this one plural noun.

clue.text: Raised mark in oral exam makes you twirl about

indicators.note: an oral exam is spoken, so the word is taken by its pronunciation

blocks.note: a wheal is a raised red mark on the skin, a welt

explanation.surface: A high grade in a spoken test sends a student spinning with joy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised mark' suggests a grade going up, but it is a welt on the skin, spelt WHEAL or WEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To wheel is to turn round or pivot, as soldiers or birds do, so it matches spinning around.

clue.text: Opposition member’s article Congress backed

indicators.note: something backed runs from the back, so the letters go the other way

blocks.note: the indefinite article
it is a coy word for sexual intercourse, a sense of congress

explanation.surface: An opposition politician writes a piece that Congress then supports.
explanation.walkthrough: Congress looks like the American legislature, but it means sexual intercourse, which crosswords often call IT.
explanation.definitionFit: An anti is a person opposed to something, so any member of an opposing side fits the noun.

clue.text: People eager to drop habits?

blocks.note: surface reading: people keen to give up bad routines such as smoking
setter's reading: habits are garments, as a nun or monk wears, so these people shed their clothes

explanation.surface: People keen to kick their bad routines.
explanation.walkthrough: A habit is also a robe, and riding habits are clothing, so dropping habits means taking clothes off.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturists prefer to go without clothing, so they gladly shed every garment.

clue.text: Not sure what to go for: Rocky or True Lies?

definitions.text: Not sure what to go for

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady and shaky, so the letters wobble out of order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone stuck choosing between two action films for movie night.
explanation.walkthrough: Rocky and True Lies both look like film titles, but Rocky is the signal to rearrange 'or True Lies'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being undecided and hesitant about which choice to make is the state of an indecisive, wavering person.

clue.text: Fish for ray over far end of pier

indicators.note: to be over something is to cover it, so one piece goes round another
the far end of a word is its final letter alone

blocks.note: a ray of light is a beam
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: An angler fishing for a ray off the end of a pier.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray looks like the flat fish, but it is a beam of light; the fish being sought is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bream is a deep-bodied freshwater or sea fish, a common catch for anglers.

clue.text: A large old queen eating with old king

indicators.note: whatever eats takes something inside itself

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
EX means former, and ER is the royal cipher for a queen
with and and both mean together with

explanation.surface: A big former queen dining with an ancient monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, so an ex-queen is EX + ER, which swallows the word for 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Several Scottish rulers and the Macedonian conqueror called the Great bore this name, so it fits a monarch of long ago.

clue.text: A great looming shifting mass

indicators.note: shifting things move about, so the letters change places

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A huge, menacing body, perhaps an iceberg or storm cloud, drifting closer.
explanation.walkthrough: The first three words are the letters to rearrange, all of them, read straight through; only the last word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: An agglomeration is a jumbled heap or cluster gathered together, which is a mass in the sense of a collected lump.

clue.text: Ghost in closet startled IT workers

indicators.note: startled people jump about, so the letters are jolted out of place

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Computer staff given a fright by a ghost lurking in a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: IT workers look like part of the scene, the people startled, but they are the definition; IT is information technology.
explanation.definitionFit: Staff in information technology are specialists in applied scientific tools, which is what technologists are.

clue.text: Saw drunk with porters and shorts?

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone saw tipsy railway porters knocking back pints and spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: Porter is a dark beer and shorts are spirits, so the surface is a drinking session; shorts are actually clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorts are casual garments for exercise and games, one example of athletic clothing.

clue.text: Two points linked by bridge?

blocks.note: surface reading: two places on either side of a river joined by a crossing
setter's reading: compass points, the seats North and South or East and West at the card game bridge

explanation.surface: Two places on opposite riverbanks joined by a crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge is the card game, whose players are named after compass points, and North pairs with South as a team.
explanation.definitionFit: In the card game, the players sitting opposite each other form a team and play together as a pair.

clue.text: People inside university meeting Liberal official

blocks.note: people inside prison are convicts, cons
U is the standard abbreviation for university
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: Members of a college get together with a Liberal Party officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People inside university' reads as students, but 'inside' means in jail, so the people are convicts.
explanation.definitionFit: A consul is a government official posted abroad to look after citizens, or a chief magistrate of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Dope artist and lad brought up for high singers

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing letters up makes them read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a sop is a feeble, foolish person
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
a son is a lad

explanation.surface: A drug-taking painter and a boy reared to be choristers.
explanation.walkthrough: Dope suggests drugs, but it means a fool. RA, Royal Academician, is a common crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: The soprano part is the highest vocal range, so its performers are the choir's top-pitched voices.

clue.text: Out-of-time president of America might create this

definitions.text: Out-of-time president of America might create this

indicators.note: out of means without, so the letter for time is dropped

blocks.note: Donald Trump, the American president
T is the abbreviation for time
US is the United States

explanation.surface: A president past his time in office might stir up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the president minus his T, then US, and the uproar such a figure might cause.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a noisy commotion or uproar, the sort of fuss a controversial leader could stir.

clue.text: Cuts of fish

blocks.note: first meaning: haircuts short at the front and long at the back
second meaning: grey or red sea fish

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a fishmonger's fillets, but the cuts are hairstyles.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a hairstyle cropped in front but long behind and a family of edible coastal fish.

clue.text: Company opening filled by a new contract

indicators.note: something filled has other material put inside it

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
a vent is an opening that lets air out
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A firm's job vacancy taken by someone on a fresh contract.
explanation.walkthrough: Opening looks like a job vacancy, but it is a hole for air.
explanation.definitionFit: A covenant is a formal binding agreement, especially one in a deed, so it is a kind of contract.

clue.text: A home for soldiers

blocks.note: surface reading: barracks or a veterans' residence
setter's reading: soldier is the name for a caste of large-jawed insects that guard a colony

explanation.walkthrough: Barracks spring to mind, but soldiers here are insects defending their nest.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldier insects live in a mound of earth built by the colony, which is their nest.

clue.text: Pompous Tory leader plans of merit confused

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the first letter counts
confused things are mixed up, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A pompous Conservative Party leader unveils muddled policies he thinks are worthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory leader' looks like a politician, but it only supplies one letter to the jumbled mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A pompous person has an inflated sense of their own importance and dignity, the meaning of this hyphenated adjective.

clue.text: Bit quiet, you say?

indicators.note: saying is speaking, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: peace and quiet mean the same calm

explanation.surface: Someone checking whether something is a little on the quiet side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit quiet' reads as 'rather quiet', but it splits into the definition and the clue to the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A bit and a piece are both a portion or fragment of something larger.

clue.text: Don’t go and mention cuddling teddy at the front

indicators.note: to cuddle is to hold in one's arms, so one piece wraps another
the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: to mention is to say
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A child begs someone not to leave and to speak of the teddy bear they are hugging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't go' is a whole command standing for one word, and 'and' joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone not to leave is asking them to remain where they are, an imperative synonym.

clue.text: Republican jealous with first lady being constantly in Vogue

blocks.note: Eve was the first woman in the Bible
R is the abbreviation for Republican
green with envy means jealous

explanation.surface: A Republican envious that the president's wife always features in a fashion magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: First lady looks like a president's wife, but it is the first woman of Genesis, and 'with ... first' puts her at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evergreen never goes out of fashion and stays popular year after year, like a plant that keeps its leaves.

clue.text: Stupid writer put one into end of sentence

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; the clue's adjective is used informally, as in 'idiot behaviour'

indicators.note: to put something into another is to place it inside

blocks.note: the writer of the clue refers to themselves as I
a sentence ends with a full stop, a dot
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A foolish author jams a single word onto the close of a sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupid writer' reads as one insult; the setter is the writer, so the second word is I.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiot is a foolish person, and the word is used attributively for anything daft.

clue.text: One might be spotted heading away from accident

indicators.note: the head of a word leaving means its first letter goes

blocks.note: a crash is an accident

explanation.surface: A witness may be seen fleeing the scene of a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' suggests being seen; it is covered in spots, which some skin eruptions are.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash is an outbreak of red marks on the skin, so it may well be spotty.

clue.text: I believe backsliding saleswoman and boyfriend must be split up!

indicators.note: to slide backwards is to go the opposite way, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: a rep is a sales representative
split into its halves: a boy is a son, and a friend is an ally

explanation.surface: Someone insists a relapsing saleswoman should break up with her boyfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split up' looks like a breakup, but it tells you to split 'boyfriend' into its two halves, each clued separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'personally' introduces one's own view, so it stands for 'in my opinion' as a sentence opener.
